pos: n. (the Augustinian priory on the Yorkshire coast, founded 1113, whose last prior was hanged after the Pilgrimage of Grace)
etymology: Old English Bredlingtun, the estate of Berhtel's people; the Domesday form is Bretlinton.
biblical_def: Bridlington Priory was founded about 1113 by Walter de Gant for canons regular of St Augustine, and became the wealthiest Augustinian house in Yorkshire. Its best-known member was John of Thwing, prior from 1362 until his death in 1379, canonised in 1401 as John of Bridlington — the last Englishman canonised before the Reformation. The shrine drew pilgrims and the revenue that went with them. In 1537, after the rising known as the Pilgrimage of Grace, the last prior William Wood was hanged at Tyburn for his part in it, and the priory was suppressed; the nave alone was left standing, and it serves as the parish church to this day. The dictionary records Bridlington for the shape of that ending, because the half-ruin is an honest picture of what the house had become: a nave where a congregation still heard preaching, attached to a choir, a shrine and a revenue that had to go. “But one thing is needful” (Luk 10:42) is the sentence the Reformers set against the whole establishment, not because labour and learning are nothing, but because the one needful thing had been buried under the rest. A shrine that sells access to a dead prior cannot give what “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) offers freely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priory as a convent of lower rank than an abbey; a canon as a church dignitary living under a rule; a shrine as a case for sacred relics; a pilgrim as a wanderer to a holy place; and needful as necessary.
webster_full: PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; an altar or a tomb of a reputed saint.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; particularly, one that travels to visit a holy place, or relics of a reputed saint.
NEEDFUL, a. Necessary, as a supply or expedient; requisite.
scriptures: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: The richest Augustinian house in Yorkshire, whose last prior was hanged in 1537 and whose nave survives as a parish church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Christ named in Bethany, where a woman busy with many good things was told that “But one thing is needful” (Luk 10:42) and that the better part was to sit and hear. Bridlington had a library, a shrine, a hospital and an income. What it could not sell, and what the surviving nave still offers, is the invitation “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28).

The live temptation is to read the suppression as mere plunder, which much of it was, and to conclude that nothing needed reforming. The priory's own economy answers that. Pilgrims came to a tomb for benefit, and Scripture reserves that traffic to no shrine: “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9). The men of faith in Hebrews are commended for owning no holy ground at all, having “strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) for their description.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a sojourner, a resident alien; “strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

“strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — the saints owned no holy ground.

pos: n. (the Augustinian priory in Cleveland founded c. 1119 by Robert de Brus, among the richest in the north of England)
etymology: Old Norse Gigr with Old English burh, a stronghold; the medieval spelling is commonly Gisburn or Gyseburne.
biblical_def: Guisborough Priory was founded about 1119 by Robert de Brus, lord of Skelton and ancestor of the Scottish royal line, for Augustinian canons. It grew into one of the richest religious houses in northern England, holding wide estates in Cleveland and the North York Moors. A catastrophic fire in 1289, started by a plumber working on the roof, destroyed much of the church and most of its books; the east end rebuilt afterwards is the great arch that still stands. The house was dissolved in 1540. The dictionary records Guisborough for the fire and the library, since a house whose treasure was a building and a book-collection learned in one afternoon how little of it would last. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.” (Isa 40:8) is not a sentiment about gardens; it is the measure the prophet applies to everything a man can own, set against the one thing that cannot burn. The canons rebuilt the arch. What the Reformers recovered was that the word itself had never needed rebuilding, because “Thy word is true from the beginning” (Psa 119:160).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbey as a monastery governed by an abbot; a library as a collection of books; to wither as to fade or dry up; a treasure as wealth laid up; and endurance as continuance.
webster_full: ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion and celibacy.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve.
ENDURE, v.i. To continue in the same state without perishing; to last; to remain.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever.
Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: One of the richest Augustinian houses in the north, burned in 1289 with most of its books, rebuilt, and dissolved in 1540.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophet's measurement of permanence. Guisborough lost its church and its library to a roofing accident, and the sentence that fits the ash is “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.” (Isa 40:8). The Psalmist says the same of the text itself, that “Thy word is true from the beginning” (Psa 119:160), which is why the Reformation could be a recovery rather than an invention.

The live temptation is nostalgia for the vanished house, as though the arch on the skyline were the loss. The canons themselves would have known better from their own Gospel: the scribe instructed unto the kingdom is the man who “bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” (Mat 13:52), holding both and clutching neither. Hebrews says flatly that “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14), and a burned priory is only that verse proved early.

pos: n. (the Augustinian priory in Coxwold, Yorkshire, founded 1145, home of the chronicler William of Newburgh)
etymology: Old English niwe and burh, the new stronghold; Latinised in the chronicles as Novoburgum.
biblical_def: Newburgh Priory in Coxwold was founded in 1145 by Roger de Mowbray for Augustinian canons, who moved there from Hood near Thirsk. Its lasting importance is a book rather than a building. William of Newburgh, a canon of the house, wrote between about 1196 and 1198 the Historia Rerum Anglicarum, a history of England from the Conquest to his own day, and he wrote it as a man who checked things. He is remembered above all for refusing Geoffrey of Monmouth's British legends on the ground that they were unsupported, and for saying so plainly. The priory was dissolved in 1538 and the buildings passed to Anthony Belasyse. The dictionary records Newburgh for William's method, which is the historian's form of a duty Scripture lays on every hearer. The Bereans were commended not for agreeing but because they “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and the apostle's rule is the same instrument: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). A canon who would not take a chronicle on its word was doing, in his own field, what “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) requires of a minister.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a register of events in order of time; to search as to look over carefully; to prove as to try or ascertain; a fable as a fictitious narration; and credible as worthy of belief.
webster_full: CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to examine by inspection.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.
FABLE, n. A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fiction; a falsehood.
CREDIBLE, a. That may be believed; worthy of credit; as a credible witness.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
corruption_summary: Augustinian priory at Coxwold, founded 1145, whose canon William of Newburgh wrote a history that refused unverified legend.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that verification is a Christian duty and not a modern invention. The Bereans were called more noble precisely because they “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and Paul commands the same posture of a whole congregation: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). William of Newburgh, declining to repeat a story he could not support, was obeying that rule in the only field he had.

The live temptation runs the other way, toward a credulity that treats any old account as venerable because it is old. The apostle names the alternative to kept doctrine as babbling, charging Timothy to “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings” (1Ti 6:20). An elder's qualification is the same discipline turned into teaching, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), which is a sentence about a text and not about a tradition's age.

pos: n. (the Augustinian priory on the Derwent in Yorkshire, founded c. 1122 by Walter l'Espec, founder also of Rievaulx)
etymology: Old Norse kirkja with Old English ham, the church settlement; the Domesday form is Chercan.
biblical_def: Kirkham Priory was founded about 1122 on the banks of the Derwent by Walter l'Espec, the Yorkshire baron who six years later gave Rievaulx to the Cistercians. The two foundations of one man make Kirkham unusually instructive, because in the 1130s the Augustinian canons of Kirkham and the Cistercians of Rievaulx negotiated over which of them certain brethren would join, and the draft agreement survives. It is a plain document about men choosing between two rules, two diets and two styles of worship, and it shows how much of medieval religion turned on such choices. Kirkham is remembered now for its great carved gatehouse, raised about 1290 and covered with heraldry. The priory was dissolved in 1539. The dictionary records Kirkham for the gatehouse and the agreement together, since a house that advertised its patrons' arms on the way in had already answered a question Scripture answers differently. The apostle allows no such ranking of orders: “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) is said of all believers, and “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5) makes the building out of people rather than people out of the building.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gatehouse as a house over a gate; a rule as a prescribed guide for conduct; heraldry as the art of armorial bearings; a priesthood as the office of a priest; and an order as a religious fraternity.
webster_full: GATE, n. A large door which gives entrance into a walled city, a castle, a temple, or any inclosure.
RULE, n. That which is established as a principle, standard or directory; a prescribed guide for conduct or for action.
HERALDRY, n. The art or office of a herald; the art, practice or science of recording genealogies and blazoning arms.
PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest; the order of men set apart for sacred offices.
ORDER, n. A religious fraternity or society; a body of men united by some common rule.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Augustinian priory on the Derwent, founded c. 1122 by the founder of Rievaulx, known for its heraldic gatehouse of c. 1290.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one priesthood. Kirkham and Rievaulx divided men by rule and habit, and Peter divides them not at all, writing to ordinary scattered Christians that they are “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9). The building metaphor runs the same way: “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5), so that the stones are the people and no gatehouse confers rank.

The live temptation is to admire the arms over the door as harmless decoration. It was never quite harmless, because it answered the question of whose house it was. Paul answers that question with a foundation and a corner stone, “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20), and leaves no masonry for a patron's crest. Where that is settled, order is still required but it is the congregation's order, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40).

pos: n. (the Durham priory on the Wear raised over the hermitage of Godric, who died there in 1170)
etymology: Old English finc and halh, the finches' nook or corner of land; pronounced locally without the middle syllable.
biblical_def: Finchale lies in a loop of the River Wear below Durham. Godric, a Norfolk man who had been a pedlar and a sea-trader and had sailed to Jerusalem, settled there about 1110 with the bishop's leave and lived as a hermit for some sixty years until his death in 1170. His life was written by Reginald of Durham, who knew him, and it preserves two short English hymns Godric is said to have sung — among the earliest surviving English verse set to music. After his death the site became a cell of Durham Cathedral Priory, and from the fourteenth century it served as a holiday house where monks from Durham came in rotation. It was dissolved in 1538. The dictionary records Finchale for the slide from hermitage to rest-house, which is an honest sequence rather than a scandal. Solitary prayer has the Lord's own example: “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) and “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.” (Luk 5:16) describe withdrawal as a rhythm, not a vocation. What Scripture never does is turn the nook into a career or a merit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hermit as one who lives in solitude; a cell as a small cave or religious house subordinate to another; solitary as living alone; devotion as the act of worship; and a vow as a solemn promise to God.
webster_full: HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.
CELL, n. A small cave or cavern; a small or mean place of residence; a religious house subordinate to a larger.
SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company; retired; remote from society.
DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated, consecrated, or solemnly set apart for a particular purpose; the act of worship.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a promise of something to be given or done.
scriptures: Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Luk 5:16
And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.
Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone.
corruption_summary: Hermitage of Godric on the Wear, died 1170, which became a cell and later a rest-house of Durham Cathedral Priory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that withdrawal for prayer is a rhythm and not a rank. The Gospels record it of Christ repeatedly: “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35), and again “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.” (Luk 5:16). He went and He returned, and the going is commended while the staying is never commanded.

The live temptation is to make the nook itself holy, which is exactly what happened at Finchale when a hermit's cave became a shrine and then a monks' holiday house. Christ locates the whole business indoors and out of sight: “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). A man may climb a hill to pray, since “he went up into a mountain apart to pray” (Mat 14:23), but the hill earns him nothing.

pos: n. (the Lancashire Cistercian abbey of 1296, whose abbot John Paslew was executed in 1537 for the Pilgrimage of Grace)
etymology: Old English hwael and leah, the clearing by the round hill; recorded in Domesday as Wallei.
biblical_def: Whalley Abbey in the Ribble valley was not founded on its site but moved to it. The Cistercian community had been planted at Stanlow on the Mersey in 1178, a flood-prone and miserable place, and in 1296 it transferred to Whalley, where an ancient parish church already stood with its Saxon crosses in the yard. Building went on for well over a century. The abbey's end was violent: the last abbot, John Paslew, took part in the Pilgrimage of Grace, the northern rising of 1536 against the suppression of the smaller houses and the religious changes behind it, and he was tried and executed in March 1537. Whalley was dissolved that year. The dictionary records Whalley for the rising and the execution, and declines to make the abbot either a hero or a villain. The rebels asked for the old religion, and their instinct that something was being torn up by the roots was not wrong, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.” (Pro 22:28) being a real command. But the paths a man is told to ask for are specified, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the old way in Jeremiah is the text, not the custom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; a landmark as a mark of boundaries; a rising as an insurrection; ancient as old or of long standing; and a path as a way beaten by feet.
webster_full: PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey which a person takes to visit some holy place, as to the sepulchre of Christ at Jerusalem.
LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm, a town, or an estate may be known.
INSURRECTION, n. A rising against civil or political authority; the open and active opposition of a number of persons.
ANCIENT, a. Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time.
PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey moved from Stanlow in 1296, dissolved in 1537 after its last abbot joined the Pilgrimage of Grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between an old path and an old habit. The rebels of 1536 were defending something, and Scripture does forbid casual demolition: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.” (Pro 22:28). But Jeremiah's famous verse names what is to be asked for, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the good way there is a way to walk in, revealed, not merely inherited.

The live temptation is to settle the question by force, which both sides tried. Zechariah had already ruled that out for the rebuilding of a house of God: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). And the doctrine actually at stake in the 1530s was not a boundary stone but a sentence, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), which is why the rising could not have saved what it wanted to save.

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) — neither side was entitled to settle it by force.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey in Ribblesdale founded 1148, suppressed in 1536, briefly reoccupied during the Pilgrimage of Grace)
etymology: Old English salh and leah, the willow clearing; the medieval form is commonly Salley or Sallay.
biblical_def: Sawley Abbey in Ribblesdale was founded in 1148 by William de Percy as a daughter house of Newminster, and it was poor from the start. The valley was wet, the harvests failed, and the community more than once petitioned for relief; in the 1320s it was so reduced that the monks were temporarily dispersed. Sawley was suppressed in 1536 under the act against the lesser houses, and then, during the Pilgrimage of Grace that autumn, the monks returned and resumed services with local support. That restoration lasted months. The abbot, William Trafford, was executed in 1537. The dictionary records Sawley for the reoccupation, because it is the clearest case in the north of ordinary people wanting their abbey back. Their attachment was real and it deserves to be said plainly rather than explained away. It was also attachment to a system that had taught them to buy what cannot be bought, and the Reformed answer is not contempt for their affection but the sentence that frees it: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) following immediately so that no house, poor or rich, stands between a sinner and God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suppression as the act of putting down; to restore as to bring back to a former state; grace as the free favour of God; a boast as a vaunt; and poverty as destitution of property.
webster_full: SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, putting down, crushing or destroying; the act of concealing.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former place or state; to bring back; to repair; to re-establish.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
BOAST, v.i. To vaunt one's self; to brag; to glory; to speak with ostentation.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: Poor Cistercian house in Ribblesdale, suppressed 1536 and briefly reoccupied by its monks during the Pilgrimage of Grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel answers attachment with something better rather than with scorn. The people of Ribblesdale wanted their monks back, and the sentence that meets them is “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), immediately guarded by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) so that nothing in the transaction depends on a house surviving.

The live temptation is to treat the 1536 reoccupation as proof that the Reformation was imposed from above against a contented people. Much of the suppression was greed, and saying so costs nothing. But the doctrine at issue was stated in a single clause, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), and Paul puts it negatively in the same breath, “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). A poor abbey could not supply what that clause denies to every abbey.

pos: n. (the South Yorkshire Cistercian abbey of 1147, whose plundering in 1538 was described by an eyewitness)
etymology: From Old French roche, a rock, for the limestone cliffs of the valley; Latinised de Rupe.
biblical_def: Roche Abbey was founded in 1147 in a narrow limestone valley in South Yorkshire by Richard de Busli and Richard FitzTurgis, as a daughter house of Newminster. It is remembered less for its history than for its ending, because Michael Sherbrook, rector of nearby Wickersley, wrote in the next generation an eyewitness account of the dissolution of 1538 drawn from men who had been there. He describes the lead stripped and melted with the carved timber of the choir for fuel, the service books torn up for scrap, and his own father carrying away a piece of it; and he asks the countrymen why they helped, and reports the answer, that they did it because they might as well have the profit as another. The dictionary records Roche for that answer. Sherbrook's account is the plainest evidence that much of the suppression was theft dressed as reform, and the dictionary says so. It does not follow that the house should have stood, only that “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) indicts the method, and that the men who melted the lead were not advancing “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) but taking a profit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plunder as goods taken by force; sacrilege as the violation of sacred things; covetousness as an inordinate desire of wealth; spoil as that which is seized; and repentance as sorrow for sin with amendment.
webster_full: PLUNDER, v.t. To pillage; to spoil; to strip; to take the goods of an enemy by open force.
SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religious uses.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; an inordinate desire of wealth.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.
REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, with a sincere purpose of amendment.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey in a limestone valley, founded 1147, whose 1538 plundering Michael Sherbrook recorded from eyewitnesses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a right end does not sanctify a greedy means. Sherbrook's neighbours stripped Roche for the profit, and Zechariah's word over a rebuilding is exactly contrary: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). Where reformation is real it looks like Ephesus being told to “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), a return to doing, not a sale.

The live temptation is to use Roche to discredit the Reformation as such, which confuses the doctrine with its hangers-on. The doctrine was Paul's warning against a religion of human tradition, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). The test of the men who carried off the lead is the one James gives, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27), and by that test they failed as plainly as any monk they displaced.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey in Wensleydale, settled 1156, famed for horse-breeding; its abbot was executed in 1537)
etymology: Norman French Jorvalle, the valley of the Ure, Latinised Jorevallis; the modern spelling keeps the French vaulx.
biblical_def: Jervaulx Abbey took its present site in Wensleydale in 1156, the community having moved from Fors higher up the dale, and it was a daughter of Byland. Its monks became noted horse-breeders, running stud and pasture across the dale, and the abbey is also credited in local tradition with the origins of Wensleydale cheese. The last abbot, Adam Sedbergh, was drawn into the Pilgrimage of Grace, it appears reluctantly and under pressure from the commons; he was nonetheless convicted and executed at Tyburn in 1537, and his name is still to be seen scratched into the wall of the Beauchamp Tower in the Tower of London. Jervaulx was dissolved and its stone widely robbed. The dictionary records Jervaulx for the stud and the scratched name together, since the house shows the medieval monastery at its most ordinary — a large farm with a choir attached. Scripture honours that labour without crowning it: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is said to all the saints, and “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is said to all of them too, in neither case to a habit or an order.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines husbandry as the business of a farmer; a stud as a collection of breeding horses; labour as exertion of body or mind; steadfast as firmly fixed; and vain as empty or fruitless.
webster_full: HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising and management of stock.
STUD, n. A collection of breeding horses and mares, or the place where they are kept.
LABOUR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; toil; work.
STEADFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly fixed or established; constant; resolute.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary work without a special religious class to perform it. Jervaulx bred horses and made cheese, and Paul's promise over such labour is given to every believer: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). The same breadth governs the exhortation, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9), which is addressed to a whole congregation in Galatia and to no order at all.

The live temptation is to suppose that work becomes holy by being done inside a cloister. The Psalmist asks instead that God “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17), which is a prayer any ploughman may pray on his own ground. And the companionship a monastery institutionalised is commended by Solomon as plain wisdom for anyone, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” (Ecc 4:9).

pos: n. (the small Premonstratensian abbey above the Tees in County Durham, founded c. 1195)
etymology: Old English Egleston, Egel's farmstead; unrelated to ecclesia despite the look of the name.
biblical_def: Egglestone Abbey stands above the Tees near Barnard Castle, founded about 1195 by Ralph de Multon for Premonstratensian canons — the white canons, an order that lived under a rule stricter than the Augustinians' and served parishes as well as choirs. Egglestone was always small and always poor. Its income was repeatedly reported insufficient, it suffered from Scottish raiding after Bannockburn, and more than once the abbey asked to be reduced in status. At the dissolution in 1540 there were a handful of canons left. The buildings passed into a private house and then into ruin. The dictionary records Egglestone for its smallness, because the medieval system is usually described from its great houses and most of its houses were like this one. A dozen men on a thin income, saying offices above a river, are a better picture of the whole than Fountains or Rievaulx. Scripture neither mocks nor flatters them. “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10) honours the humblest place in God's house, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) denies that the humility earns anything.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon regular as one living under a rule; poverty as want of means; a doorkeeper as one who guards an entrance; humility as freedom from pride; and merit as desert of reward.
webster_full: CANON, a. (regular) One who lives according to a rule, as distinguished from a secular canon not so bound.
POOR, a. Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence.
DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
scriptures: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Small, poor Premonstratensian house above the Tees, founded c. 1195 and dissolved in 1540 with only a few canons left.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the lowest place in God's house is a good place and not a meritorious one. The Psalmist chooses it outright, “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10), and the choice is affection rather than accounting. Egglestone's few poor canons occupied something like that place for three and a half centuries.

The live temptation is to let poverty itself do the work of righteousness, which is the error the white canons' rule was always close to. Paul refuses it for himself in the sharpest terms, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), and the alternative he names is a righteousness received. Hence the governing sentence for a poor house and a rich one alike: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).
